raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|viceroy|6748|Vicksburg group}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|A ''viceroyal'' government was expressly created for it [Buenos Ayres, in 1777].
{{right|''Mrs. Horace Mann'', Life in the Argentine Repub., p. 122.}}}}

'''viceroyalty''' (vīs-roi′al-ti), ''n.'' [= F. ''viceroyauté''; as ''viceroyal'' + ''-ty''.] The dignity, office, or jurisdiction of a viceroy. ''Addison.''
{{smaller block|Upon the question of the ''Viceroyalty'' there might be a difference of opinion. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XIX. 38.}}}}

'''viceroyship''' (vīs′roi-ship), ''n.'' [< ''viceroy'' + ''-ship''.] The dignity, office, or jurisdiction of a viceroy; viceroyalty. ''Fuller.''

'''vice-sheriff''' (vīs-sher′if), ''n.'' A deputy sheriff.
{{smaller block|Sir William Martyn, who had been elected . . . knight of the shire for Devon, petitioned the council against the undue return made by the ''vice-sheriff'', who had substituted another name. {{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 423.}}}}

'''vice-treasurer''' (vīs-trezh′ṳ̄r-ėr), ''n.'' A deputy or assistant treasurer.

'''vice-treasurership''' (vīs-trezh′ṳ̄r-ėr-ship), ''n.'' [< ''vice-treasurer'' + ''-ship''.] The office or duties of a vice-treasurer.
{{smaller block|So many things are vacant and no acceptors: Treasury, Navy vacant; ''Vice-Treasurership'' of Ireland, with several other things that is amazing, goes begging.
{{right|Quoted in ''The Academy'', March 7, 1891, p. 225.}}}}

'''vicety†''' (vī′se-ti), ''n.'' [< ''vice''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ty'' (after ''nicety'', etc.).] Fault; defect; imperfection.
{{smaller block|Old Sherewood’s ''vicety''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Love’s Welcome at Welbeck.}}}}

'''vice versa''' (vī′sē vėr′sä̤). [L.: ''vice'', abl. of *''vix'', change, alternation, alternate order (see ''vice''<sup>4</sup>); ''versā'', abl. fem. of ''versus'', pp. of ''vertere'', turn, turn about: see ''verse''<sup>1</sup>.] The order being changed. {{smaller|The phrase has the complete force of a proposition, being as much as to say that upon a transposition of antecedents the consequents are also transposed.}}
{{smaller block|This very important paper is an investigation of the simple illusion which makes a light weight lifted after a heavy one seem disproportionately light, and ''vice versa.''
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Psychol.'', II. 650.}}}}

'''vice-warden''' (vīs-wâr′dn), ''n.'' A deputy warden.
{{smaller block|Seawen, a Cornish writer and ''Vice-Warden'' of the Stannaries.
{{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXII. 690.}}}}

'''Vicia''' (vis′i-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Rivinus, 1691), < L. ''vicia'', a vetch: see ''vetch''.] A genus of leguminous plants, the vetches, of the suborder ''Papilionaceæ'', type of the tribe ''Vicieæ''. {{smaller|It is characterized by a stamen-tube oblique at the apex, an ovary with many (rarely with two) ovules, and a style which is mostly filiform and more or less beaked, usually with a terminal dorsal tuft. About 200 species have been described, of which probably not over 100 are well defined. They are widely distributed through north temperate regions and South America; one species, ''V. sativa'', long cultivated, is now naturalized within the southern hemisphere in the Old World. They are chiefly tendril-climbers, rarely spreading herbs, or somewhat erect. The flowers are usually blue, violet, or yellowish. The fruit is a compressed two-valved pod with globose seeds. The species are known in general as ''vetch''. ''V. sativa'' is cultivated in the Old World as a fodder-crop, also under the names of ''fitches'', ''tares'', and ''lints''; 16 or more other species are also useful for forage. (See ''tare''<sup>2</sup>.) Several species are valued for their seeds, especially ''V. Faba'' (''Faba vulgaris''), the horse-bean of Old World cultivation (for which see ''Faba'', ''bean''<sup>1</sup>, ''Mazagan''). ''V. gigantea'' (''V. Sitchensis''), a tall, robust purple-flowered climber growing from San Francisco to Sitka, produces seeds which when young resemble green peas in size and taste. Nine species are natives of England, 72 of Europe, about 10 in the United States, besides a few in Mexico; 3 species (mentioned under ''tare'') are locally naturalized in the United States; 3 only are native to the Central States, of which ''V. Americana'' (see ''pea-vine'') extends west, ''V. Cracca'' north, and ''V. Caroliniana'' east; the last, the Carolina vetch, is a delicate plant with graceful secund racemes of small lavender flowers; ''V. Cracca'', the tufted vetch, or cow-vetch, is also native in the Old World, and is much admired for its densely flowered racemes, which are first blue, and turn purple. See cuts under ''Faba'', ''mucronulate'', ''plumule'', ''pod'', and ''vetch''.}}

'''viciate†''', ''v. t.'' An obsolete spelling of ''vitiate''. ''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 636.

'''Vicieæ''' (vi-si′ẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Bronn, 1822), < ''Vicia'' + ''-eæ''.] A tribe of leguminous plants, of the suborder ''Papilionaceæ''; the vetch tribe. {{smaller|It is characterized by a herbaceous stem, leaves abruptly pinnate, continued into a simple or branching tendril or bristle, and with their leaflets commonly minutely toothed at the apex. Their stipules are usually foliaceous, oblique, or half-sagittate; their flowers axillary and few, solitary or racemed; their seeds with a funiculus expanded above, the cotyledons thick and fleshy and not appearing above the ground in germination. The 6 genera include most of the plants known as ''pea'' and ''vetch''—the genera ''Cicer'', ''Lens'', and ''Pisum'' belonging exclusively to the Old World, ''Vicia'' (the type), ''Lathyrus'', and ''Abrus'' also to the New.}}

'''vicinage''' (vis′i-nāj), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''voisinage'' (the form ''vicinage'' being made to agree with ''vicinity'', etc.); < OF. ''voisinage'', ''veisinage'', F. ''voisinage'', neighborhood, < ''veisin'', F. ''voisin'', near, {{smaller block|{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xii.}}
I live in a ''vicinage'' beloved by nightingales, and where they often keep me awake at night.
{{right|''Mortimer Collins'', Thoughts in my Garden, II. 104.}}}}
'''2.''' The condition of being a neighbor or of being neighborly.
{{smaller block|Civil war had broken up all the usual ties of ''vicinage'' and good neighbourhood.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Common because of vicinage.''' See ''common'', 4.}}

'''vicinal''' (vis′i-nal), ''a.'' [< F. ''vicinal'' = It. ''vicinale'', < L. ''vicinalis'', neighboring, < ''vicinus'', neighboring: see ''vicine''.] Near; neighboring. [Rare.]—{{smaller|'''Vicinal planes,''' in ''mineral.'', planes whose position varies very little from certain prominent fundamental planes: for example, the planes of the cube in fluor-spar are sometimes replaced by the vicinal planes of a tetrahexahedron, which are very nearly coincident with those of the cube, and hence are called ''vicinal''.—'''Vicinal surface.''' See ''surface''.}}

'''vicine†''' (vis′in), ''a.'' [= OF. ''veisin'', F. ''voisin'' = Sp. ''vecino'' = Pg. ''vizinho'' = It. ''vicino'', < L. ''vicinus'', near, neighboring (as a noun ''vicinus'', m., ''vicina'', f., a neighbor), lit. ‘of the (same) village, quarter, or street,’ < ''vicus'', a village, quarter of a city, street: see ''wick''.] Same as ''vicinal''.
{{smaller block|For duetie and conscience sake towards God, vnder whose mercifull hand nauigants aboue all other creatures naturally bee most nigh and ''vicine''.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 229.}}
Pride and envy are too uncivil for a peaceable city; the one cannot endure a ''vicine'' prosperity, nor the other a superior eminency.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 321.}}}}

'''vicinity''' (vi-sin′i-ti), ''n.'' [< OF. ''vicinité'' = It. ''vicinità'', < L. ''vicĭnita(t-)s'', < ''vicinus'', near, neighboring: see ''vicine''.] '''1.''' The quality of being near; nearness in place; propinquity; proximity.

{{smaller block|The abundance and ''vicinity'' of country seats.{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''2.''' Neighborhood; surrounding or adjoining space, district, or country.
{{smaller block|Gravity alone must have carried them downwards to the ''vicinity'' of the sun.{{right|''Bentley'', Sermon vii., A Confutation of Atheism.}}
Communipaw . . . is one of the numerous little villages in the ''vicinity'' of this most beautiful of cities [New York].{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 100.}}}}
'''3.''' Nearness in intercourse; close relationship.
{{smaller block|Their [the bishops’] ''vicinity'' and relation to our blessed Lord.{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Episcopacy Asserted, § 40.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Proximity'', etc. See ''neighborhood''.}}

'''viciosity''' (vish-i-os′ị-ti), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''viciositee''; < L. ''vitiosita(t-)s'', < ''vitiosus'', vicious: see ''vicious''.] Depravity; viciousness; vice; lack of purity, as of language or style. Also spelled ''vitiosity''.
{{smaller block|In which respect it may come to passe that what the Grammarian setteth downe for a ''viciositee'' in speach may become a vertue and no vice.{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 129.}}}}

'''vicious''' (vish′us), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''vitious''; < ME. ''vicious'', < OF. ''vicious'', ''vitious'', ''vicieus'', F. ''vicieux'' = Pr. ''vicios'' = Sp. Pg. ''vicioso'' = It. ''vizioso'', < L. ''vitiosus'', faulty, vicious, < ''vitium'', fault, vice: see ''vice''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Characterized by vice or imperfection; faulty; defective.
{{smaller block|Some ''vicious'' mole of nature.{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4. 24.}}
Their [the logicians’] form of induction . . . is utterly ''vicious'' and incompetent.{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}
If a creature be self-neglectful, and insensible of danger, or if he want such a degree of passion in any kind as is useful to preserve, sustain, or defend himself, this must certainly be esteem’d ''vitious'', in regard of the design and end of Nature.
{{right|''Shaftesbury'', Inquiry, II. i. § 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Mannerism is pardonable, and is sometimes even agreeable, when the manner, though ''vicious'', is natural.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Boswell’s Johnson.}}}}

'''2.''' Addicted to vice; habitually transgressing moral law; depraved; profligate; wicked.

<poem>Happy the Roman state, where it was lawful,
If our own sons were ''vicious'', to choose one
Out of a virtuous stock, though of poor parents,
And make him noble.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, i. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Wycherley . . . appears to have led, during a long course of years, that most wretched life, the life of a ''vicious'' old boy about town.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Comic Dramatists of the Restoration.}}}}

{{smaller block|“I know his haunts, but I don’t know his friends, Pendennis,” the elder man said. “I don’t think they are ''vicious'' so much as low.”
{{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, v.}}}}

'''3.''' Contrary to moral principles or to rectitude; perverse; pernicious; evil; bad.

{{smaller block|For which cause Richard Iohnson caused the English, by his ''vicious'' liuing, to bee worse accounted of then the Russes.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 391.}}}}

{{smaller block|Every ''vicious'' action must be self-injurious and ill.
{{right|''Shaftesbury'', Inquiry, II. ii., Conclusion.}}}}

{{smaller block|Whatsoeuer transgressed those lymits, they counted it for ''vitious;'' and thereupon did set downe a manner of regiment in all speech generally to be obserued, consisting in sixe pointes.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 130.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is a ''vicious'' use of speech to take out a substantive kernel from its content and call that its object.
{{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychology, I. 275.}}}}

'''6.''' Not well broken or trained; given to objectionable tricks: said of an animal.

{{smaller block|He was, in fact, noted for preferring ''vicious'' animals, given to all kinds of tricks, which kept the rider in constant risk of his neck.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 439.}}}}

'''7.''' Characterized by severity; virulent; malignant; spiteful: as, a ''vicious'' attack. [Colloq.] {{smaller|—'''Vicious circle.''' See ''circle.''—'''Vicious intromission.''' See ''intromission'', 3.—'''Vicious syllogism,''' a fallacy or sophism.—'''Vicious union,''' the knitting of the two fragments of a broken bone in such a way as to cause deformity of the limb or marked interference with its function. ='''Syn. 2''' and '''3.''' ''Wicked, Depraved'', etc. (see ''criminal''), unprincipled, licentious, profligate.—'''6.''' Refractory, ugly.}}

'''viciously''' (vish′us-li), ''adv.'' In a vicious manner. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In a manner contrary to rectitude, virtue, or purity: as, a ''viciously'' inclined person. (''b'') Faultily; incorrectly: as, a picture ''viciously'' painted. (''c'') Spitefully; malignantly: as, to attack one ''viciously''.}}

'''viciousness''' (vish′us-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being vicious. {{smaller|(''a'') The quality or state of being imperfect; faultiness; imperfection; defectiveness: as, the ''viciousness'' of a system or method. (''b'') Corruptness of moral principles or practice; habitual violation of the moral law or disregard of moral duties; depravity in principles or in manners.}}

<poem>When we in our ''viciousness'' grow hard.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 13. 111.}}}}

{{smaller block|The best and most excellent of the old law-givers and philosophers among the Greeks had an allay of ''viciousness.''
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 25.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Unruliness; trickiness; bad training, as of a shying or bolting horse.}}
{{smaller block|A broken-down plough-horse, that had outlived almost everything but his ''viciousness.''
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 436.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') Spitefulness; malignancy.}}

¶'''vicissitude''' (vi-sis′i-tūd), ''n.'' [= F. ''vicissitude'' = Sp. ''vicisitud'' = Pg. ''vicissitude'', < L. ''vicissitudo'', change, < ''vicissim'', by turns, < *''vix'' (''vic-''), change: see ''vice''<sup>4</sup>.] '''1.''' Regular change or succession of one thing to another; alternation.
{{smaller block|God created them equall, but by this it came to passe that the ''vicissitude'' or intercourse of day and night was vncertaine.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 260.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Grateful ''vicissitude'', like day and night.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 8.}}}}
'''2.''' A passing from one state or condition to another; irregular change; revolution; mutation: as, the ''vicissitudes'' of fortune.
{{smaller block|But it is not good to look too long upon these turning wheels of ''vicissitude'', lest we become giddy.
{{right|''Bacon'', Vicissitudes of Things (ed. 1887).}}}}
{{smaller block|His whole life rings the changes — hot and cold, in and out, off and on, to and fro: he is peremptory in nothing but in ''vicissitudes.''
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 505.}}}}
{{smaller block|As long as there are Men, there must be malignant Humours, there must be Vices, and ''vicissitudes'' of Things.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sometimes ’tis grateful to the rich to try
A short ''vicissitude'', and fit of poverty.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Horace’s Odes, I. xxix. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|But ''vicissitudes'' so extraordinary as those which marked the reign of Charles the Second can only be explained by supposing an utter want of principle in the political world.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}}

{{smaller block|The whirlpool of political ''vicissitude'', which makes the tenure of office generally so fragile.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 12.}}}}

'''vicissitudinary''' (vi-sis-i-tū′di-nạ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< L. ''vicissitudo'' (''-din-''), vicissitude, + ''-ary''.] Subject to vicissitudes; exhibiting or characterized by a succession of changes; vicissitudinous.
{{smaller block|We say . . . the days of man [are] ''vicissitudinary'', as though he had as many good days as ill.
{{right|''Donne'', Devotions, p. 313.}}}}

'''vicissitudinous''' (vi-sis-i-tū′di-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''vicissitudo'' (''-din-''), vicissitude, + ''-ous''.] Characterized by or subject to a succession of changes; vicissitudinary.

'''Vicissy duck.''' [< ''Vicissy'', a local name (cf. Sp. ''vicicilin'', a humming-bird), + E. ''duck''<sup>2</sup>.] The widow-duck. ''Simmonds.''

'''Vicksburg group.''' In ''geol.'', a division of the Tertiary, of importance in the Gulf States from Florida west to Mississippi. {{smaller|The name ''Vicksburg'' was given by Conrad, who referred this group to the Oligocene, a reference which has been confirmed by Heilprin, who, however, prefers the name ''Orbitoidal'', given with reference to the great abundance of ''Orbitoides Mantelli'', the most distinctive fossil of these beds.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
